prompt: Registering a new application in Microsoft Entra ID creates which two linked objects?
choices: A global application object and a service principal
A service principal and a managed identity
An enterprise application and a Conditional Access policy
An application object and a security group
correctAnswers: A global application object and a service principal
explanation: Registration produces the global application object — the blueprint — plus a service principal, its local identity in this tenant. A managed identity is the tempting third name in that list, whereas it is a separate identity type created on an Azure resource rather than by registering an app.

prompt: Where do you configure an app's redirect URIs, client secrets/certificates, and the API permissions it requests?
choices: App registrations
Enterprise applications
Managed identities
Conditional Access
correctAnswers: App registrations
explanation: App registrations is where the blueprint lives: redirect URIs, secrets and certificates, and the API permissions the app requests. Enterprise applications is the closest miss and governs the resulting service principal — assignments, single sign-on, consent — whereas the credentials belong to the registration.

prompt: In which blade do you assign users/groups to an app, enable single sign-on, and review the OAuth permission grants that have actually been consented?
choices: Enterprise applications
App registrations
Roles and administrators
Identity Governance
correctAnswers: Enterprise applications
explanation: Enterprise applications governs the app's service principal within your tenant. App registrations is where permissions are declared/requested, not where consent state is governed.

prompt: A single multi-tenant app registration is used by 40 customer tenants. How many service principals exist for it across those tenants?
choices: One service principal per consuming tenant
None until an admin creates them by hand in each tenant
Exactly one, shared across all of the tenants
One per user who signs in to the app
correctAnswers: One service principal per consuming tenant
explanation: The application object is global, but each consuming tenant gets its own service principal (created on consent) that it governs locally.

prompt: Which permission type lets an app act on behalf of the signed-in user, bounded by what that user can do?
choices: Delegated permissions
Application permissions
Directory role permissions
Data-plane RBAC permissions
correctAnswers: Delegated permissions
explanation: Delegated permissions require a signed-in user and are bounded by that user's own access. Application permissions are the near neighbour and behave in the opposite way: the app acts as itself with no user present, so nothing the user could not do limits it.

prompt: A background daemon with no signed-in user needs to read all mailboxes via Microsoft Graph. Which permission type and consent apply?
choices: Application permissions, with admin consent
Application permissions that any licensed user can consent to
Delegated permissions, self-consented by the daemon
Delegated permissions requiring no consent at all
correctAnswers: Application permissions, with admin consent
explanation: With no signed-in user the daemon must use application permissions, and those always require admin consent. Delegated permissions self-consented by the daemon is the tempting invention, whereas there is no user in the flow to do any consenting.

prompt: Why do application permissions always require admin consent, regardless of how narrow the permission is?
choices: There is no signed-in user to consent on their own behalf
They are always classified as high-impact by Microsoft
They can only be granted at the tenant root management group
They require a verified publisher, and only admins can verify publishers
correctAnswers: There is no signed-in user to consent on their own behalf
explanation: Application permissions require admin consent because the app acts as itself, with no signed-in user who could consent on their own behalf. Being classified high-impact is the tempting explanation, however the reason is structural rather than a matter of risk rating — it holds even for the narrowest permission.

prompt: To stop users from consenting to risky third-party apps while still allowing low-risk cases, you restrict user consent to verified publishers and low-impact permissions. What handles the rest?
choices: The admin consent workflow, routing to reviewers
A Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for the app
A resource lock on the enterprise application object
Automatic denial of all the remaining requests
correctAnswers: The admin consent workflow, routing to reviewers
explanation: The admin consent workflow lets users request access and routes it to reviewers/admins, rather than silently blocking legitimate needs.

prompt: Where is the tenant-wide user consent policy (verified publishers, low-impact permissions) configured?
choices: Enterprise applications ▸ Consent and permissions
Microsoft Entra ID ▸ Roles and administrators blade
App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets
Privileged Identity Management ▸ Settings
correctAnswers: Enterprise applications ▸ Consent and permissions
explanation: The tenant-wide user consent policy and the admin consent workflow both live under Enterprise applications ▸ Consent and permissions. App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets is the closest miss and governs one app's credentials, whereas consent policy is a property of the tenant.

prompt: Which statement best describes a service principal?
choices: The local identity of an app in one tenant
The global, tenant-independent blueprint of an application
A Conditional Access construct for workload identities
A group used to assign Azure RBAC roles in bulk
correctAnswers: The local identity of an app in one tenant
explanation: A service principal is the application's local, governable identity inside one tenant — what receives assignments and consent. The tenant-independent blueprint is the application object, whereas the service principal is its per-tenant instance, and that pair is what these questions keep testing.

prompt: Which type of managed identity is bound to a single resource's lifecycle and deleted automatically when that resource is deleted?
choices: System-assigned
Workload-federated
User-assigned
Multi-tenant
correctAnswers: System-assigned
explanation: A system-assigned managed identity is created on one resource and deleted with it, rather than managed separately — a strict one-to-one binding. User-assigned is the near neighbour and survives independently, which is what makes it the answer whenever an identity must pre-exist a deployment or be shared.

prompt: Which type of managed identity exists as its own standalone Azure resource and can be attached to several resources at once?
choices: User-assigned
Workload-federated
System-assigned
Delegated type
correctAnswers: User-assigned
explanation: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone Azure resource, attachable to several resources at once and surviving all of them. System-assigned is the tempting default because it is one toggle, whereas it cannot be shared or created ahead of the resource it belongs to.

prompt: Five VMs must share exactly the same identity to reach a Key Vault, and that identity must persist even if individual VMs are rebuilt. Which identity fits best?
choices: A user-assigned managed identity attached to all five VMs
A system-assigned managed identity on each VM
A single service principal whose client secret is copied to each VM
A shared access signature distributed to each VM
correctAnswers: A user-assigned managed identity attached to all five VMs
explanation: Only a user-assigned managed identity is both shareable across the five VMs and independently lifecycled, so rebuilding a VM changes nothing. A single service principal with its client secret copied to each VM is the tempting alternative and reintroduces exactly the credential handling that managed identity removes.

prompt: Why is a managed identity preferred over a service principal with a client secret for a workload running on an Azure resource?
choices: There is no secret to store, leak, or rotate
It automatically grants the workload Owner on the subscription
It is the only identity type that can call Microsoft Graph
It removes the need to assign any RBAC role
correctAnswers: There is no secret to store, leak, or rotate
explanation: The benefit is credential handling and nothing else: there is no secret to store, leak or rotate, because Azure manages it. It does not grant Owner and it does not remove the need for RBAC — the identity still needs a role assignment before it can reach anything.

prompt: 'All managed identities are service principals.' Which statement about the reverse is correct?
choices: Not all service principals are managed identities
Service principals and managed identities are unrelated objects
A service principal exists only while a user is signed in
All service principals are managed identities
correctAnswers: Not all service principals are managed identities
explanation: Every managed identity is implemented as a service principal, but ordinary app registrations also have service principals whose secrets/certs are your responsibility.

prompt: An app registration's client secret is about to expire and outages occur when it lapses. Which change most durably eliminates this class of problem for an Azure-hosted workload?
choices: Replace the service principal with a managed identity
Store the client secret in Key Vault and read it at startup
Add a second client secret as a backup credential
Set the client secret so it never expires
correctAnswers: Replace the service principal with a managed identity
explanation: Replacing the secret-based service principal with a managed identity removes the expiry problem entirely, because there is no secret to expire. Vaulting the secret or adding a backup is the tempting improvement, whereas both still leave a credential to rotate — the outage is postponed rather than prevented.

prompt: What is an OAuth permission grant, as seen under an enterprise application?
choices: A record that a permission was actually consented
An Azure RBAC role assignment on a resource group scope
A certificate uploaded to the app registration
A Conditional Access rule applied to the app
correctAnswers: A record that a permission was actually consented
explanation: An OAuth permission grant records that a delegated or application permission has actually been consented for the service principal, which is distinct from being merely requested in the registration. An Azure RBAC role assignment is the tempting neighbour, however it governs Azure resources rather than API permissions.

prompt: You want to prevent a specific enterprise application from being usable except by an approved pilot group. What should you configure?
choices: Require user assignment, assign the pilot group
Set a ReadOnly resource lock on the application object
Add a NotActions entry to the app's service principal
Delete the application's client secret
correctAnswers: Require user assignment, assign the pilot group
explanation: Enterprise applications support 'Assignment required?' plus user/group assignment, restricting who can use the app. Locks and NotActions do not apply to enterprise-app usage.

prompt: An Azure Function must read a secret from Key Vault with no stored credentials. What should it use, and what else is required?
choices: A managed identity, plus a Key Vault data role
The Key Vault admin account credentials in app settings
A managed identity alone — no role assignment needed
A shared access signature for the Key Vault
correctAnswers: A managed identity, plus a Key Vault data role
explanation: The managed identity provides credential-free authentication, but it still needs authorization — an RBAC data role like Key Vault Secrets User (or a vault access policy).

prompt: Which statement about credential management is correct for the two managed-identity types?
choices: Azure rotates the credentials for both types
Only system-assigned identities are credential-free
User-assigned identities store a secret in app settings
Both require you to upload a certificate annually
correctAnswers: Azure rotates the credentials for both types
explanation: Azure creates and rotates the credential for both managed-identity types, so neither has a secret you handle. Believing only system-assigned is credential-free is the trap: the two differ in lifecycle and shareability, whereas the credential story is identical.

prompt: A developer added an API permission in App registrations, but the app still can't call the API. What is the most likely missing step?
choices: Consent has not been granted for the requested permission
The app registration must be converted to an enterprise application
A managed identity must be enabled on the app
The permission must be added again under Certificates & secrets
correctAnswers: Consent has not been granted for the requested permission
explanation: Requesting a permission is not the same as being granted it — a user or admin must consent before the app can exercise it.

prompt: Which is the correct place to rotate or remove a compromised client secret for a registered application?
choices: App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets
Managed identities ▸ Federated credential list
Enterprise applications ▸ Users and groups
Key Vault ▸ Access configuration
correctAnswers: App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets
explanation: Client secrets and certificates for a registered app live under App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets, which is where a compromised one is rotated or removed. Enterprise applications ▸ Users and groups is the closest miss and governs who may use the app, whereas the credential belongs to the registration.

prompt: Which approach lets an external workload (e.g. a GitHub Actions pipeline) authenticate as an Entra app WITHOUT a stored client secret?
choices: Workload identity federation on the registration
Embedding a long-lived client secret as a repository secret
A user-assigned managed identity attached to GitHub
A shared access signature scoped to the app
correctAnswers: Workload identity federation on the registration
explanation: Workload identity federation lets an external IdP's token be exchanged for an Entra token, removing the stored secret. Managed identities apply to Azure-hosted resources, not GitHub.

prompt: A user-assigned managed identity is attached to a VM, then the VM is deleted. What happens to the identity?
choices: It survives and can be attached elsewhere
It is converted into a system-assigned identity instead
It is disabled until re-attached within a day
It is deleted along with the VM itself
correctAnswers: It survives and can be attached elsewhere
explanation: A user-assigned identity is independent of any single resource, so deleting the VM leaves it intact and reattachable elsewhere. Expecting it to be deleted with the VM is the confusion with system-assigned, whereas that independence is the whole reason the type exists.

prompt: Which two statements about a system-assigned managed identity are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Its lifecycle is tied to a single resource
It is deleted automatically with that resource
It can be attached to multiple resources at once
It requires a client secret that you rotate
correctAnswers: Its lifecycle is tied to a single resource
It is deleted automatically with that resource
explanation: A system-assigned identity is bound one-to-one with its resource and deleted automatically with it. Neither remaining option holds: it cannot be attached to several resources, which is a user-assigned capability, and it has no client secret for you to rotate.

prompt: Which two are true about consent in Microsoft Entra ID? (Choose two.)
choices: Application permissions need admin consent
User consent can be limited to verified publishers
A standard user can grant admin consent for application permissions
Delegated permissions can never be consented by a user
correctAnswers: Application permissions need admin consent
User consent can be limited to verified publishers
explanation: Application permissions always require admin consent, and user consent can be narrowed to verified publishers and low-impact permissions. A standard user can never grant admin consent, whereas low-risk delegated permissions can be user-consented — which is why the other two statements are false.

prompt: Which two objects govern the SAME application but at different scopes? (Choose two.)
choices: The application object (blueprint)
The service principal (local identity)
A network security group rule set object
A Key Vault secret value entry
correctAnswers: The application object (blueprint)
The service principal (local identity)
explanation: The application object is the global blueprint and the service principal is its local tenant instance: one application, two objects at different scopes. A network security group and a Key Vault secret are tempting only as familiar Azure nouns, whereas neither has anything to do with application identity.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (a background invoicing daemon with no signed-in user must read data from Microsoft Graph), which permission and consent are required?
choices: Application permissions with admin consent
Delegated permissions with user consent
Delegated permissions with no consent
No permissions — daemons bypass Graph authorization
correctAnswers: Application permissions with admin consent
explanation: The invoicing daemon runs with no signed-in user, so it needs application permissions, which always require admin consent. Delegated permissions with user consent is the tempting answer, however there is no user in the flow to consent or to bound the access.

prompt: Referring to requirement 4 (a deployment pipeline running on an Azure VM must reach Key Vault with no stored client secret), which is the correct design?
choices: A managed identity, plus a secrets-read data role
Store a service principal client secret in the pipeline's variables
Generate a Key Vault SAS token and hard-code it in the pipeline
Use the Key Vault admin account credentials
correctAnswers: A managed identity, plus a secrets-read data role
explanation: A managed identity on the VM plus a Key Vault secrets-read data role gives credential-free access, so nothing is stored on the machine. Storing a service principal client secret in the pipeline environment is the tempting familiar pattern, whereas it puts the credential exactly where requirement 4 forbids it.

prompt: Contoso's security team wants to ensure employees can no longer consent to arbitrary third-party apps on their own, while still letting legitimate requests reach IT. What should they configure?
choices: Restrict user consent and enable the admin consent workflow
Delete all existing enterprise applications
Require MFA for the Microsoft Graph cloud app
Assign every employee the Cloud Application Administrator role
correctAnswers: Restrict user consent and enable the admin consent workflow
explanation: Restricting user consent stops arbitrary approvals; the admin consent workflow routes genuine needs to administrators instead of blocking them outright.

prompt: Order the steps to give an Azure Function a credential-free way to read a Key Vault secret.
reorderItems: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the Function app
Note the managed identity's object ID
Assign it the Key Vault Secrets User role scoped to the Key Vault
Reference the secret from application code via the Key Vault SDK/reference, with no credential in code
explanation: The identity must exist before it can be granted a role, and the role must be assigned before code can successfully read the secret. Granting the role first is not merely poor ordering but impossible: there is no principal ID to name in the assignment yet.

prompt: Order the steps to register an application and let it call Microsoft Graph as a daemon with admin-consented application permissions.
reorderItems: Add the required application permission under API permissions
Have an administrator grant admin consent for the tenant
Generate a client secret or certificate for the app
Use the client credentials flow to obtain a token
explanation: The permission must be requested and consented before the client credentials flow can return a usable token. Generating the credential and testing before consent is the ordering mistake, and it fails as an authorization error rather than an authentication one — which is what makes it confusing to debug.

prompt: Configure this simplified API permissions screen for a daemon service (no signed-in user) that must read all users' profiles via Microsoft Graph.
explanation: No user is signed in, so application permissions are required; reading every user's profile needs User.Read.All; and application permissions always need admin consent. Delegated permissions is the trap in this screen, because the app still authenticates successfully whereas every Graph call then fails.

prompt: Proposed solution: Create a service principal with a client secret and store the secret in an environment variable on the VM. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: A secret is still stored on the VM, in an environment variable, which the goal explicitly forbids. It is tempting because it works — the pipeline does reach Key Vault, however working was never the constraint; not storing a credential was.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the VM and grant it a Key Vault Secrets User role. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: The managed identity needs no stored credential on the VM or in code, and Key Vault Secrets User authorizes exactly the read access required. Note the prerequisite it carries: the vault must use the RBAC access model, whereas a legacy access-policy vault would need a policy entry instead.

prompt: Proposed solution: Generate a long-lived SAS-style token for the Key Vault and embed it in the job's configuration file. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: This is still a stored, long-lived credential in configuration — Key Vault authorization doesn't work this way, and it fails the 'no stored credential' requirement either way.

prompt: Which Azure CLI command enables a system-assigned managed identity on an existing VM?
choices: az vm identity assign
az identity create
az vm extension set
az ad sp create-for-rbac
correctAnswers: az vm identity assign
explanation: `az vm identity assign` turns on the identity that lives and dies with the VM. `az identity create` is the closest miss and creates a standalone USER-assigned identity instead — same feature family, whereas the lifecycle it produces is the opposite one. `az ad sp create-for-rbac` would create a service principal with a client secret, reintroducing exactly the credential a managed identity removes.

prompt: Which command creates a USER-assigned managed identity as a standalone resource?
choices: az identity create
az vm identity assign
az ad sp create-for-rbac
az ad app create
correctAnswers: az identity create
explanation: A user-assigned identity is its own Azure resource, so it is created on its own with `az identity create` (PowerShell: New-AzUserAssignedIdentity) before any VM references it. `az vm identity assign` is the inverse operation and attaches an identity to a VM rather than creating a standalone one; neither `az ad` command produces a managed identity, they register applications.

prompt: Which PowerShell cmdlet creates a user-assigned managed identity?
choices: New-AzUserAssignedIdentity
New-AzUserAssignedIdentityConfig
New-AzADServicePrincipal
New-AzManagedIdentity
correctAnswers: New-AzUserAssignedIdentity
explanation: New-AzUserAssignedIdentity is the dedicated cmdlet. New-AzADServicePrincipal creates a classic service principal (credentials to manage); the other two don't exist.

prompt: Which command creates a service principal for automation AND assigns it a role in one step?
choices: az ad sp create-for-rbac
az role assignment create
az identity create
az ad app create
correctAnswers: az ad sp create-for-rbac
explanation: `az ad sp create-for-rbac` does four things at once: registers the application, creates the service principal, generates a credential, and assigns the role given by `--role` and `--scopes`. `az role assignment create` is the tempting miss and only does the last of those — the principal must already exist. Note what this command is not: it emits a client secret, which is why an Azure-hosted workload should use a managed identity instead.

prompt: A VM's system-assigned managed identity must read secret values from Key Vault KV1, which uses the Azure RBAC access model. Complete the role assignment.
explanation: Key Vault Secrets User is the data-plane role that reads secret VALUES. Key Vault Reader is the trap: it reads vault and secret metadata but never the value, so the workload authenticates, lists the secret, and still fails to read it. Secrets Officer adds write and delete, which is more than reading needs, and plain Reader is control-plane only. The scope is the vault, not the VM: the assignment says who may read this vault, not what the VM may do. On a legacy access-policy vault the equivalent step would be `az keyvault set-policy` instead — mixing the two models leaves a second, unaudited source of access.
